The saying is usually a joke or a shrug. It is neither when it is your life. The work went well. You carry more than you did ten years ago: people, payroll, decisions, a reputation that took years to build and could be lost in an afternoon. You may still have friends who have walked with you the whole way up. And still there may be no one who knows the whole of what you carry. Here is the honest answer: the top does not make a man lonely. Carrying it alone does. The loneliness is usually a sign that you have become isolated inside your own life, and that you need support you have not let yourself ask for.

Why It Is Lonely Up There

It is not a character flaw, and it is not a sign you chose the wrong work. It is what happens when a man's responsibilities grow faster than the number of people he lets see him. The people who report to you need you steady, and some things should not be said in that room. That is wise. The trouble starts when the same editing follows you everywhere else: to the friends who have known you for years, to home, to church. You hand them the public version because it is easier, and in time the editing becomes the loneliness. The people are often still there. They have stopped being let in.

The desire underneath the climb is good. The want to build, to provide, to be the one who can be counted on, to leave something that holds: that is a God-given desire, and the Bible honors it. The counterfeit feeds that good desire a lie: that being counted on means never needing anyone. Build on it long enough and you have a company, a church or a family that works, and a man inside it who is unknown.

What the Bible Says About the Man Who Has No One

Ecclesiastes does not look away from this. “One person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, ‘For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?’ This also is vanity and an unhappy business” (Ecclesiastes 4:8). The man is not failing. He is succeeding, and his success has no one in it. The next lines are the answer, and they are not about working less: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10). The Bible's worry for the man at the top is not that he will stop climbing. It is that he will fall with no one close enough to reach him.

Then there is Elijah. In 1 Kings 18 he wins the most public victory of his life on Mount Carmel. One chapter later he is running, and he “came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there” (1 Kings 19:3) before going on alone into the wilderness. Under a broom tree he asks to die, and when God asks what he is doing there, he answers like every isolated man who has succeeded: “I, even I only, am left” (1 Kings 19:10). It was not true. God does not argue with the feeling. He feeds him and lets him sleep. He speaks in “a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:12), not a louder victory. Then he tells Elijah that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed, and gives him a man named Elisha to walk with him. Elijah was never as alone as he felt. He had walked away from the people who were with him, and God's answer was rest, a quiet word and a companion.

What You Can Do This Week

Start smaller than you think. This is fixed one honest sentence at a time, not by a retreat next quarter.

Tomorrow, write down the three things you are carrying that no one in your life knows in full. Not the public version. The real weight: the decision you are dreading, the fear under the confidence. Keep the page. That is the first move of a crossing, acknowledging what is true before you try to fix it.

Then name one man. Not a board member, not someone whose paycheck you sign. It may be a friend who has been with you the whole way and has only heard the public version. A man with nothing to gain from your success and nothing to lose from your weakness. Ask him for an hour this week and tell him one of the three. Not all of it. One. Tell him you are not asking for advice; you are asking to be known. Most men are honored to be asked.

If no one comes to mind, say so to yourself plainly. It is not a verdict on you. It is a measure of how isolated the work has made you, and it is the place to start. It can be the first thing you tell our team.

Where Story, a Group and a Witness Come In

The loneliness is a signal that the way you have been known no longer fits the life you now carry. That is a threshold, and in the Bible a threshold is where God tends to meet a man, not wasted ground. On this path we call it a crossing: acknowledge the ending, wait with purpose, invest wisely, and rise. The work is done through your story, told a piece at a time, with men doing the same.

A small group of men is the fastest way through, and the one most men at the top avoid longest. It is where Ecclesiastes 4 happens: the man who has fallen has another to lift him. In our groups a man says what is true, and no one in the room reports to him. If you have never sat in one, start by telling one man.

On our paths, a man does not walk alone. He walks with a witness. A witness is someone who sees what God is doing in your story, so it is remembered and spoken back to you. Your witness walks your road with you: one person, who reads what you choose to share and writes to you. At first that is your group's leader or our team; then you invite your own: a mentor, a coach, a close friend, a pastor or a relative. It is Ecclesiastes 4 made practical: someone close enough to reach you, who knows what you carry because you chose to tell them.
